title: Proof Before Price: Pre-Registered Behavioral Tests of Proof-Based Pricing on Language-Model Buying Agents
abstract: Pricing theory assumes a buyer who can be persuaded. When the buyer is a delegated languagemodel agent, a seller's claims reach an evaluation procedure, and the pricing question is whether that procedure admits an offer, rewards what it can verify, and reads a price schedule differently from a posted price. This paper reports, to the author's knowledge, the first pre-registered, frozen-code test of verification, legibility, and schedule effects on language-model buying agents: three hosted frontier models (gpt-5, gemini-3.6-flash, claude-sonnet-5) and one openweight model (Qwen3.6-27B) run locally. Agents chose among twelve synthetic offers, or none, in a frozen marketplace under five yoked manipulations; of 168,816 records, 166,389 were analyzed with code frozen before any scored query. Three hypotheses were registered (OSF, DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/GPBUK): admission as a legibility threshold, a verified premium, and a schedule effect at equal price. The verified premium and the schedule effect hold on every agent © 2026 Paul F. Accornero. Licensed under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. 2 at the registered levels. An offer whose claim can be checked in a register is selected 14 to 30 percentage points more often than the same claim in prose; a missing register identifier costs 15 to 29 points; an executable schedule stating its terms is selected 7 to 33 points more often than the same price posted. One registered sub-prediction, stated from the design of the channels before any such measurement existed, is not supported: the registration expected a machineattested claim to be selected at or above a certified one, and on three of the four agents the attested claim is selected 6 to 12 points less often, with no detected difference on the fourth. This paper reports that result as the field's move from observation to quantification. The admission threshold does not hold: the labels-only offer is considered every time and selected about as often as the structured one, with selection falling smoothly with price, the registered refuting observation. Effect sizes differ by agent; the local model's are the smallest on the verification and schedule members, though not on the labels-only contrast or the chatter arm.
why: Pre-registered LLM buying agents, frozen code, 168k records

title: NumTrace: Auditing the Number Provenance of Financial Analyst Agents
abstract: A numerical claim generated by a financial analyst agent can match a number in a company filing but refer to the wrong entity, concept, period, unit or scope. A check based on reference answers can mark such an answer as wrong but does not explain why it fails. In this paper, we present NumTrace, a new benchmark that audits the provenance of each numerical claim made by financial analyst agents: its source and financial semantics. NumTrace currently has 540 questions over 2,163 SEC EDGAR documents. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first numerical benchmark about who holds a company's shares (Form 13F) and what its executives are owed (Item 402(i)). On a frozen snapshot of these documents, we build the reference answers according to accounting rules. NumTrace then gives each claim three separate verdicts: value, binding and support. By retaining separate value and binding verdicts, NumTrace detects right number, wrong account (RNWA) errors: a claim has an RNWA error when it passes the value check but fails the binding check. The RNWA rate quantifies the gap between value-only and joint value-and-binding pass rates. Finally, we audit three agents, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. RNWA errors make up 67.5-81.8% of each agent's failing claims. In particular, on 13F co-filing group questions, about 91% of claims pass the value check, but fewer than half pass the binding check.
why: Financial analyst agent benchmark over SEC EDGAR filings

title: Risk-proportional inference: Constraint-aware model routing for fair and energy-efficient financial AI serving
abstract: Financial institutions serve millions of scoring requests with heavyweight machine-learning models whose inference cost dominates serving energy budgets, while remaining subject to fair-lending and model-risk obligations. Cost-aware model routing reduces this cost but optimizes accuracy-cost trade-offs only, and can silently worsen group fairness. We formulate responsible model routing for financial serving as online constrained optimization: minimize inference energy subject to a risk-proportionality rule that always assigns the champion model to high-stake requests, a fairness non-inferiority band on the cumulative statistical parity difference, and an accuracy non-inferiority floor relative to the best deployable static configuration. We instantiate the formulation with RAIRoute, an online controller combining an uncertainty gate, group-signed flip-rate projections, an exactly tracked counterfactual budget, and a latched breach-recovery mode, generalized to multi-group protected attributes. Across five public serving streams from three tabular datasets, RAIRoute holds the fairness band while cutting per-request energy by up to 70.9% on the fairness-binding stream, refuses to trade accuracy for savings where the accuracy floor binds, and detects infeasible fairness bands online. A five-seed, five-ordering robustness study shows that constraint feasibility varies across training runs, elevating serving-time monitoring from safeguard to core control function: a bootstrap study with oracle ground truth shows the latch-based detection signal recovers 95.1% of infeasible configurations, and four-metric fairness analysis shows why selection-rate control cannot substitute for offline error-rate monitoring. Every decision emits an auditable reason code, supporting model-risk and AI-Act-style governance.
why: Constrained model routing for financial AI serving, practical

title: Thinking-in-Bets at Test Time Reduces Sycophantic Revisions in LLM Agents
abstract: Language model agents often abandon correct work when a user challenges it, yet simply telling them to stand firm makes them ignore real mistakes. Once an agent reads a complaint, it tends to discount its own earlier checks in order to agree with the user. We introduce Thinking-in-Bets, a training-free method in which an agent writes a short private record of its main claims, the checks supporting them, and its confidence before reading user feedback. When challenged, the agent consults this Claim Checklist to keep verified work intact while investigating uncertain or newly challenged parts. We evaluate five Gemini models (3.5 Flash-Lite, 3.5 Flash, 3.6 Flash, 3.8 Flash, and 4.0 Argon) across eight benchmarks: SWE-Together, SWE-Interact, and DeepSWE for software engineering, Agents' Last Exam for professional reports, Humanity's Last Exam and SycEval for academic reasoning, Vals Finance for financial analysis, and Terminal-Bench for command-line tasks. Recording claims before criticism nearly eliminates false reversals in patch review and protects passing report drafts under mistaken pushback, whereas writing the same record after reading the complaint recovers very little of the gain. In multi-turn coding, pre-reply claim records substantially reduce unnecessary file edits after mistaken complaints, and gating the record so it is written only when the agent is uncertain lowers token overhead while fixing more real bugs than the baseline. Even in non-interactive tasks without user feedback, listing the key claims in a draft and re-checking the weakest one before submission improves both answer accuracy and confidence estimates across all tested models.
why: Training-free LLM agent method with Vals Finance benchmark

title: Do Round Numbers Hold Prices? Occupation Densities and Depth-Conditioned Hazards in the Limit Order Book
abstract: Prices cluster at round numbers, a pattern often interpreted as evidence that these levels act as price barriers. This pattern also admits a mechanical explanation: more liquidity rests there, and prices take longer to leave deeper queues. Limit order book data allow us to distinguish these mechanisms through a tick-grid framework in which local time counts departures and level-wise volatility reflects the departure hazard. Using data for five Nasdaq stocks throughout 2025, we find that round levels attract more liquidity but do not exhibit longer depth-adjusted durations. Intel and SoFi show directional effects, with departures biased away from round levels.
why: Limit-order-book microstructure using real Nasdaq 2025 data

title: LLM-Enhanced Heterogeneous Graph Learning with Business Semantics for Financial Fraud Detection
abstract: Financial fraud detection increasingly relies on heterogeneous transaction graphs, in which entities such as cards and merchants play distinct business roles and the risk meaning of an attribute depends on the entity's role: a high transaction volume may be routine for a merchant but unusual for a card. Heterogeneous graph neural networks preserve typed entities and relations but typically treat these attributes as role-agnostic inputs and leave their business meaning implicit. Meanwhile, most existing methods integrating large language models (LLMs) with graphs focus on homogeneous graphs or heterogeneous graphs with naturally available textual attributes, leaving their use on transaction graphs with structured attributes underexplored. To address this issue, we propose SemHGT, an LLM-enhanced framework that interprets structured attributes according to entity roles and makes the business semantics explicit in three stages: (1) role-aware prompts elicit risk-related business descriptions from node attributes, and a text encoder maps them to semantic vectors that enrich node representations; (2) semantic similarity guides multi-round sampling of target-specific path instances under transaction-to-transaction schemas; (3) schema-level tokens that combine local path evidence with global neighbor summaries are processed together with the target transaction by a unified transformer. Across three benchmark datasets, SemHGT leads the evaluated baselines on most dataset--metric comparisons. Further analyses provide additional evidence for the effectiveness of SemHGT's design and clarify how its semantic modeling and evidence selection contribute to fraud detection. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SemHGT-528A/.
why: LLM-enhanced heterogeneous graphs for financial fraud detection

title: Certifying Reward Alignment in Portfolio Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Financial reinforcement learning often translates an investment objective into an additive risk-adjusted reward. An agent can optimise that reward accurately yet implement a different financial preference. We develop a decision audit for terminal mean-variance equilibrium that separates reward misspecification from learning error. In a finite exogenous-state market, we bound the gain from changing one action using actor, reward and continuation-critic residuals. The certificate ignores state-constant critic offsets, accommodates convex action constraints, and has an independent-sample extension that does not require the equilibrium policy. A continuation-aware actor-critic method estimates the future-policy correction from samples. Across nine controlled markets and twenty seeds, it reduces policy distance by and one-step deviation gain by relative to a matched myopic-reward network. A separate PPO comparison tests the same reward intervention within a standard optimiser. Historical tests cross seven covariance estimators and 10, 30 and 49 US industry portfolios over 432 months: joint reward calibration preserves each fitted mean-variance target, but does not improve realised investment performance. Together, these results provide a way to quantify whether a learned decision implements its stated financial objective, separately from how well that objective performs in a backtest.
why: Portfolio RL reward alignment audit, controlled markets

title: Arya Forge: Auditing Validation and Release Approval for Financial Instruction Data
abstract: Financial instruction-data pipelines must distinguish content validity from permission to release a particular dataset. Arya Forge combines typed records, current-content checks, and approval coverage bound to a dataset manifest. We evaluate its release boundaries in a financial-data systems case study. An integrity audit covers 100,000 synthetic instruction records; a separate arithmetic implementation agrees with all 15,000 numeric records across twelve formula families. In 240 scenarios with 2,400 treatment rows, adding financial and release-record checks to a short-instruction filtering recipe rejects all injected numeric faults and policy holds while retaining 220 of 240 clean controls. The twenty lost controls comprise every tested cash-conversion-cycle example. Nineteen persisted-release cases show that eleven selected negative cases are blocked, four equivalent representations are rejected, and changes to external evidence after binding are outside ordinary Gold promotion's checks. Local processing measurements and controlled checkpoint resumptions characterize cost and recovery through 100,000 input rows. The results expose a tradeoff between strict producer-contract enforcement and useful-representation retention, and identify the protected inputs required for manifest-bound approval. These findings apply to the tested implementation and workloads; they do not establish general financial correctness, authenticated approval, expert-validated quality, or downstream model improvement.
why: Financial instruction-data audit, synthetic records and checks

title: A Multi-Asset Dataset and Tail-Risk Framework for DeFi Yield Trading Derivatives
abstract: Yield trading has emerged as a pivotal innovation in Decentralized Finance (DeFi) by decoupling principal from yield streams to enhance capital efficiency. Despite its significance, the field lacks fine-grained datasets for systematic empirical analysis. We address this gap by constructing the first large-scale benchmark dataset for Pendle, the pioneering on-chain interest rate derivatives protocol, spanning 24 months across 340 active markets with complete lifecycle observations. Our analysis reveals a structural market transition toward stablecoin-dominated "flight-to-quality" dynamics. To tackle the heavy-tailed nature of yield data, we propose Tail-MSE, an asymmetric loss function that prioritizes tail risk awareness through dynamic penalty weighting. Experiments across six state-of-the-art time series models demonstrate consistent improvements in volatility forecasting robustness, enabling the Tail-MSE Sniper strategy to achieve superior risk-adjusted returns in over half of all markets.
why: DeFi yield dataset and tail-risk volatility forecasting

title: Det-MASO: Diversity-Regularized Multi-Agent Sequential Optimization for Factor Generation
abstract: Quantitative investment requires alpha factors that are both predictive and diverse. However, existing factor generation methods, including formulaic mining and neural end-to-end models, are mostly based on a single-agent design, which limits exploration of the factor space and reduces adaptability to changing markets. Multi-agent approaches can broaden exploration, but agents trained under a shared objective often collapse to similar outputs, while existing diversity techniques either scale poorly with asset-universe size or address redundancy only after training. We propose a multi-agent sequential optimization (Det-MASO) framework for generating diversified, context-adaptive alpha factors. It introduces a differentiable log-determinant penalty on the inter-agent correlation matrix directly into the joint objective, discouraging correlated agent behavior during training with computational cost that scales linearly with the number of assets. We further show that this penalty prevents homogeneous equilibria and preserves factor diversity throughout optimization, while a context-conditioned scheduler dynamically adjusts agent emphasis across market regimes and Shapley interaction index analysis is used to characterize the cooperation structure that emerges among them. Experiments show that Det-MASO outperforms baselines, improving the information coefficient by 1.1\%, the annualized return by 6.4\%, and the Sharpe ratio by 0.33.
why: Multi-agent diverse alpha-factor generation

title: MINT: Mitigating Structural Inconsistency via Attentive Message Passing for Financial Anomaly Detection
abstract: Illicit account detection is a critical task for financial risk control systems, aiming to pinpoint malicious actors within transaction networks. Existing efforts typically recast transaction networks into directed multigraphs and leverage graph neural networks (GNNs) to detect anomalies via topological structures under the homophily assumption. However, directly grafting GNNs onto transaction graphs is faced with at least two pivotal challenges, i.e., structural inconsistency and label scarcity. The former arises from deceptive connections forged by malicious actors, while the latter stems from the lack of annotated data. In light of these, we introduce MINT, a novel graph neural framework that mitigates structural inconsistency via an attentive message-passing scheme on transaction graphs. Specifically, MINT introduces a discrepancy-aware feature propagation, which tracks malicious actors by quantifying deviations between nodes across bi-directional transaction flows. A transaction salience module is proposed to mitigate structural inconsistency by adaptively regularizing the interaction strength between nodes. Furthermore, to alleviate label scarcity, MINT is optimized via Positive-Unlabeled (PU) learning, which exploits only a minority of illicit nodes coupled with a majority of unlabeled ones. Extensive experiments conducted on three financial transaction benchmarks, including two large-scale public and one in-house real-world datasets, validate the superior effectiveness of MINT over several cutting-edge baselines.
why: GNN fraud detection on transaction graphs, attentive propagation

title: Scenario Matching for Credit Dependence Stress Tests: Temporal correlation constraints and empirical risk bounds
abstract: We couple two sets of simulated market and credit paths by minimizing absolute temporal-correlation error relative to a prescribed target. Each market path receives exactly one credit path, preserving both empirical distributions of complete scenarios. A perfect-matching test identifies whether a uniform correlation-error tolerance is feasible and determines its smallest attainable value. Further assignments give exact empirical mean-loss and exceedance-probability bounds; quantile bounds follow by binary search over eligible loss thresholds. A synthetic bond-forward credit stress test illustrates the method. The experiments report matching precision, empirical score tails and exposure-grid error, and measure matching and mean-loss computation. The method is independent of the scenario generator and provides a reproducible way to examine dependence assumptions in existing risk engines. Tail measures concern default-probability-weighted credit scores. Accompanying reproducibility package (Python code, synthetic scenario libraries, permutations, and benchmarks) is attached in the ZIP archive.
why: Credit stress-test scenario matching with empirical bounds

title: Weekend Crypto Volatility and Monday Market Risk
abstract: Cryptocurrencies trade continuously while major traditional markets close over the weekend. We examine whether weekend cryptocurrency volatility predicts Monday variance in equity, commodity and fixed-income markets. Using daily range-based variance measures for Bitcoin, Ether, XRP, the S&P 500, gold and a US Treasury ETF over 2017-2026, we augment heterogeneous autoregressive models with a common weekend cryptocurrency factor. Predictive content is weak before 2024 but significant thereafter. In the post-2024 sample, a one-standard-deviation increase in the factor is associated with 27-54% higher fitted Monday variance. Adding the factor reduces out-of-sample QLIKE losses by 11-22%, although statistical evidence varies across markets. Friday cryptocurrency volatility does not reproduce the result, and coin-specific variation adds no significant predictive information beyond the common factor. An endogenous procedure estimates a break in late 2023, during growing anticipation of US spot-Bitcoin ETF approval. However, ETF-flow interactions provide no evidence of amplification through greater measured Monday flow activity, leaving the mechanism unresolved. The findings suggest that calendar-specific volatility measures reveal predictive information that aggregate connectedness measures may obscure.
why: Weekend crypto volatility predicts Monday variance OOS

title: ParetoRSI-Gym: Can AI Agents Improve Language Models Across Multiple Domains?
abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) requires an agentic system to design, train, and evaluate its own successor. Data-driven post-training is a central part of that loop, yet existing evaluations measure it on a single benchmark, where an agent selects from a static pool or distills a stronger model to push one score up in one run. Real post-training is multi-domain, and a gain in one domain has to be weighed against a regression in another. We propose ParetoRSI-Gym, in which an agent searches for data, curates it, trains, reads back per-domain results, and repeats, with everything but the data held fixed: the initial LLM, the five domains (math, code, finance, medicine, science), the toolset, and the SFT pipeline. Generalization benchmarks in each domain separate capability gains from overfitting to the scores the agent optimizes against. Across three agent systems, three base models, five rounds and multiple seeds, the strongest system, Claude Code with Opus-5, raises the generalization scores of its proxy-best checkpoint by 9.2% relative to the starting model (+2.3 absolute points), averaged with equal weight over three base models and five domains, with a single-domain relative gain of up to 63% (medicine on Ministral-3-3B). Further analysis shows that the harness matters as much as the model it drives, and that each agent keeps a unique data selection strategy. We see our work as a step towards evaluation of RSI systems in real-world machine learning engineering.
why: LLM self-improvement gym, finance one of five domains

title: CoSA: The Conflict of Skills Attack in Real-World LLM Agent Ecosystems
abstract: Agent Skills allow LLM agents to combine reusable capabilities, but checking each Skill in isolation cannot rule out policy violations when they are composed. We term such failures Conflict of Skills (CoS): artifacts or assessment signals produced for one purpose may be reused downstream without preserving the restrictions or authorization needed for their new use. Using controlled executions of publicly available Skills and matched single-Skill controls, we identify four recurring mechanisms behind CoS. Building on these findings, we introduce the Conflict of Skills Attack (CoSA), which adds locally admitted Skills to an existing pool to supply missing business operations (capability supplementation) or reshape artifact exchange, decision reuse, and target/action bindings (relationship reshaping). CoSA leaves existing Skills and runtime permissions unchanged. To evaluate this threat under autonomous Skill selection, we introduce CoSA-Bench, built from real-world Skills and controlled services, with 288 tasks across recruiting, finance, IT, and business, covering data leakage, unauthorized state modification, and unsafe execution. Across five LLMs and three agent harnesses, additions capped at 5% of each original pool raise the policy-violation rate from 35.02% to 58.45%, an increase of 23.43 percentage points. Trace analysis links compliant-to-violating transitions to cross-Skill dependencies involving the additions. Finally, we develop a lightweight harness-level guard that checks information flow and authorization before consequential actions. On OpenClaw recruiting tasks across five models, the guard reduces violations from 65.28% to 6.67%, while policy-compliant task completion on matched benign controls changes from 66.67% to 65.00%.
why: LLM agent skill composition attacks, not finance-specific

title: Evolve on Graph: Self-Evolving Knowledge Graph Reasoning without Question Annotations
abstract: Knowledge graphs (KGs) provide reliable external knowledge for multi-hop factual reasoning with large language models (LLMs), yet most KGs in real-world domains such as finance and industry lack question--answer (QA) annotations. Without such annotations, existing methods struggle to improve LLM graph reasoning: training-free agents cannot improve their exploration through interaction; reinforcement learning (RL) agents depend on QA data annotated by humans or synthesized by closed-source models; and training data is typically built offline, so its topology mix is fixed and cannot follow the agent's ability. We propose Evolve on Graph (EoG), a framework that lets an LLM self-evolve its graph reasoning without any QA annotations. Through Graph Self-Play, a single LLM alternates between a Proposer that poses questions and a Solver that answers them. To make questions verifiable, Symbolically Verifiable Topology Synthesis (SVTS) samples reasoning topologies on the KG and executes the corresponding first-order logic queries, yielding topology skeletons with correct and complete answer sets; guided by a skeleton, the Proposer explores the graph to pose a multi-hop question. To let task topologies follow the Solver, a Boundary-Aware Graph Curriculum rewards the Proposer by the Solver's score variance, keeping questions at the Solver's capability boundary so that complex topologies enter training as the Solver improves. On six benchmarks over Freebase, Wikidata, and an industrial KG, EoG consistently outperforms prompting-, retrieval-, and agent-based methods, showing that LLM graph reasoning can improve through self-play without QA annotations. Our code is available at https://github.com/Szy5/EoG
why: Self-evolving knowledge graph reasoning without QA annotations

title: Fuji: The Shape, Composition, and Spread of Demand Bursts on Robinhood Chain
abstract: Demand on blockchain-based marketplaces arrives in bursts and at a high rate. On these platforms the data are completely visible, which makes it feasible to compare the bursty demand against the usual load. The congestion manifests as an increased demand for gas, the primary resource a blockchain sells. Existing studies consider how to price the gas. The demand itself, and what it is made of during bursts, has not been measured. We measure it on Robinhood Chain, a layer-2 blockchain that quickly became a venue for trading tokenized equities and memecoins. We collected the data from every block of its first three active months and more than 50 million Uniswap swaps that occurred during bursty periods. We find that a burst trades about as many pools as a quiet period, mostly different ones, and trades them harder, on top of elevated demand that accumulated for hours. With the bursts aligned on their peaks, the median peak is 2.5 times the usual load. Both the rise and the fall of the demand are described by the sum of two exponential functions with different timescales, a slow one of hours and a fast one of minutes. Against a matched quiet period, a burst has 1.05 times the pools, 1.40 times the trades, and 1.21 times the senders. We use two models to explain the arrival of bursts: externally triggered cascades and self-excitation. The former fits the data relatively better. Inside a burst, the entry of each trader into a pool is followed for about 24 seconds by more entries than the existing traders predict. Whether this is because of imitation or because of a shared signal is left open.
why: Blockchain demand burst measurement on Robinhood Chain

title: Multi-Agent Large Language Model-Based Behavior Simulation of Low-Carbon Parks in Coupled Electricity-Carbon Markets
abstract: Low-carbon parks (LCPs) differ fundamentally from traditional electricity prosumers because their heterogeneous operational behaviors and strong electricity–carbon coupling. Existing works commonly assume homogeneous behaviors or model electricity and carbon decisions separately, limiting their ability to characterize how heterogeneous LCPs form internal schedules and coupled electricity-carbon trading decisions. To address these issues, this paper proposes a multi-agent large language model (LLM)-based framework for heterogeneous LCP behavior simulation that links intra-park coordination with inter-park market interaction. Specifically, we develop a retrieval-based heterogeneity embedding method that integrates park resources, demand, and preferences into agent-usable profiles, and a physics-aware multi-round bidding and realization mechanism that converts LLM-generated decisions into executable electricity-carbon decisions during multi-round interaction and feedback. Case studies validate the framework in terms of physical feasibility and heterogeneous behavior generation in both single and multiple LCP cases. It achieves zero feasibility violations while remaining within 0.66% in cost and 0.48% in emissions of the centralized optimization benchmark. Case results also indicate that more market participation do not necessarily lead to higher system outcomes, especially with heterogeneous behaviors, highlighting the value of behavior simulation in revealing intertemporal market-design risks.
why: LLM simulation of energy-carbon parks, not finance

title: Reversion, Retention, and Semantic Intervention: Measuring Functional Content in CLIP Fine-Tuning Deltas
abstract: Fine-tuning adapts pretrained models to new tasks, but identifying which weight changes support the resulting behavior remains difficult. Weight-space interpretability assigns semantic descriptions to these changes, called fine-tuning deltas. Such descriptions leave open how much task performance depends on the identified updates, particularly when other updates can support the same predictions. We address this gap by pairing reversion, which restores selected parameters to their pretrained values, with retention, which keeps only selected fine-tuning updates. We evaluate Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) models on synthetic financial charts, Flowers102, EuroSAT, and FGVCAircraft with ViT-L/14, and on Flowers102 with ViT-B/16, using a shared recipe that tunes the final six visual blocks. Our contributions are threefold. First, attention value-output (VO) updates alone recover 43-87% of the accuracy improvement, although reverting them leaves chart accuracy unchanged. Cross-entropy loss preserves this contrast on Charts and EuroSAT, while correct-class score margins reveal additional contributions. Second, VO weights recover more loss improvement than all ten equally sized, layer-matched random subsets in each setting. VO and multilayer perceptron (MLP) retentions jointly correct 25-81% of pretrained errors, demonstrating overlapping recovered behavior, which we call operational redundancy. Third, removing semantically selected directions reduces VO-retained recovery more than matched-random removal in all five settings. Together, these results distinguish semantic alignment, removal cost, and retained recovery as complementary evidence about the functional role of fine-tuning updates within the evaluated CLIP recipe.
why: CLIP fine-tuning interpretability, synthetic finance charts only

title: Models Verify Sufficiency, Not Validity: Usable Falsehoods Evade the Checks that Gaps Trigger
abstract: Ask a model "how many settlements did the Normans control?" and it answers that the passage does not say. Tell it "given that the Normans controlled 12 settlements of 400 inhabitants, what is the total?" and it computes 4,800. Nothing was added to the passage; the unsupported fact merely became usable. Benchmarks for unanswerable questions are built almost entirely by omission, deleting the fact a question needs and scoring refusal, so they never probe this. Holding source support fixed and varying only whether an unsupported premise is usable, flagging drops 8-30 points and commitment to an answer rises 1.5-2.3x on GSM8K across four models spanning two families and 2B-26B; all 16 paired contrasts remain significant after Holm correction. Two further manipulations reproduce it, one also on SQuAD: a fact asserted rather than asked about, and a corrupted intermediate value rather than a removed one. Models articulate the exact gap they then ignore, stating that "there is no financial information provided" for an inert premise and silently adopting a fabricated price for the same item. We read these as one behaviour: whether a model checks depends substantially on whether usable material is present, even when source support is held fixed. Because the main design never instructs models to reject premises introduced in the question, adopting such a premise can also be read as conditional reasoning, and we delimit what the design does and does not show. In the judging seat the pattern differs: asked whether the answer follows, judges pass solutions with a required step deleted 78-99% of the time at every scale tested. A natural prompt-level mitigation lowers accuracy by 22 points without improving detection.
why: General LLM truthfulness eval, not financial

title: Beyond Wasserstein Proximity: Finding Better Transfer Sources
abstract: Source selection often favors similar data, yet marginal proximity need not identify the most useful pretraining source. We motivate a conditional alternative through domain-adaptation theory and a regression example in which broader source variation improves estimation despite increasing Wasserstein distance. We examine five-day cryptocurrency volatility using ten Binance spot assets, six forecaster families, three seeds, and shared temporal cutoffs. Selecting the three farthest rather than nearest Gaussian-Wasserstein sources improves mean persistence-relative skill by 12.52 percentage points for MLP and 20.90 for Transformer, with positive post-hoc paired date-block intervals. Forward pilot selection improves mean skill over random transfer in all six families. Compact recurrent models achieve the lowest absolute mean errors, separating selection utility from forecasting quality. Retrospective five-candidate screening shows additional gains from farthest-first geometry before pilot ranking for MLP and Transformer. We distinguish across-target associations from within-target decisions and evaluate target heterogeneity, training seeds, and temporal-block sensitivity. Findings are exploratory for a fixed historical panel; the screening analysis measures no runtime saving.
why: Crypto volatility transfer source selection, no trading costs

title: Can New Energy Futures Serve as Effective Hedging Instruments for AI Industry Chain Assets? Evidence from China
abstract: This paper examines the risk spillover between new energy futures and AI industry chain assets and assess the hedging value of new energy futures. We divide AI assets into upstream computing infrastructure, midstream artificial intelligence, and downstream smart manufacturing. Based on the TVP-VAR time-frequency connectedness framework, we identify significant risk spillovers across different time frequencies between new energy futures and AI industry chain assets. We find that the spillovers over short horizons being considerably stronger than those observed over medium- and long-term horizons. From the perspective of each industry chain segment, midstream artificial intelligence and downstream smart manufacturing display strong risk-output characteristics, while upstream computing infrastructure is relatively weaker in risk-output capacity. We also find that industrial silicon futures provide strong hedging effectiveness for upstream computing infrastructure assets, whereas polysilicon and lithium carbonate futures demonstrate more significant risk diversification effects when allocated with midstream artificial intelligence assets and downstream smart manufacturing assets. Therefore, incorporating new energy futures into AI industry chain portfolios can effectively reduce portfolio risk, improve hedging efficiency, and enhance risk-adjusted returns. These findings offer useful implications for investment decisions and policy formulation.
why: China-specific hedging empirics, no transferable method

title: Asymmetric time-frequency risk spillovers between the Artificial Intelligence ETFs and the Cryptocurrency market: Is economic policy uncertainty a driving factor?
abstract: This paper analyzes asymmetric spillover dynamics across time and frequency dimensions linking Artificial Intelligence ETFs and the cryptocurrency market by employing a connectedness approach built upon a time-varying parameter vector autoregressive (TVP-VAR) model. The empirical results suggests that, compared to AI ETFs, cryptocurrencies act as net sources of spillover effects. Within this process, dirty cryptocurrencies and leading green cryptocurrency assets acting as core transmitters, while artificial intelligence ETFs and certain small-cap green cryptocurrencies behave as stable net receivers. The results further reveal a clear asymmetry in spillover dynamics, with effects driven by negative news being more pronounced than those associated with positive news. In addition, the spillover effect is significantly stronger in the short term, while it weakens in the medium to long term. Dynamic analysis further indicates that major external events such as the aftermath of the Bitcoin bubble burst, the Russia-Ukraine conflict, China-US trade frictions and the COVID-19 pandemic have significantly intensified the transmission effects of risk across various markets. Finally, economic policy uncertainty exerts a positive influence on asymmetric spillover effects, suggesting that it plays a central role in driving risk spillovers. Overall, the findings of this study have significant implications, providing valuable guidance for both investors and policymakers.
why: AI ETF-crypto spillovers, no implementation pipeline

title: When AI Mistakes Invisibility for Irrelevance: A Theory of Recursive Market Exclusion in Generative-AI Marketing
abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) becomes increasingly embedded in strategic marketing, firms are relying on algorithmic representations of consumer segments to inform market research, synthetic persona generation, creative development, and advertising decisions. Yet, many consumer populations remain underrepresented in commercial tracking infrastructures, creating “data deserts” characterised by sparse, fragmented, or unobserved digital traces. When GenAI workflows encounter these information gaps without adequate domain-specific empirical grounding or uncertainty calibration, they may generate fluent, psychologically detailed consumer representations that obscure the absence of segment-specific evidence. We conceptualise this phenomenon as generative pseudocertainty and theorise how it can contribute to visibility–demand conflation : the managerial misattribution of poor campaign performance to insufficient market demand rather than to a miscalibrated marketing intervention. Integrating behavioural learning theory, performance feedback theory, and the logic of the “hot stove effect”, we develop a conceptual framework of recursive market exclusion . The framework proposes that, when marketing interventions based on uncalibrated generative representations underperform, managers may withdraw strategic investment, reducing paid exposure and the observable behavioural signals available for subsequent learning. In the absence of independent exploratory inquiry, this process may reinforce initial algorithmic invisibility and sustain the exclusion of potentially viable consumer segments. We specify a theoretical viability condition distinguishing recursive exclusion from rational market exit: exclusion is pathological when expected incremental profit under an optimal intervention remains positive (Pi* > 0), but miscalibrated generative attributes contribute to inferior realised outcomes. We derive six theoretical propositions, identify relevant boundary conditions, examine retrieval-induced representational substitution as a potential mechanism, and explain how outside-in market sensing capabilities may interrupt the proposed feedback loop. By connecting representational limitations in generative AI with managerial attribution, organisational learning, and strategic resource allocation, this paper advances a conceptual account of how AI-mediated marketing decisions may reproduce market exclusion and establishes a foundation for future empirical investigation.
why: Marketing theory, no implementation or financial data

title: Women’s Technical Agency in AI-Enabled Islamic Social Finance:Toward a Theory of Inclusive Technical Influence
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly positioned as an infrastructure for assessment, service delivery, resource allocation, and financial inclusion in Islamic Social Finance (ISF). Yet the inclusiveness of AI-enabled services is not determined only at the point of use. It is also shaped upstream through decisions about problem definition, data representation, model objectives, interfaces, testing, escalation and governance. Building on the uploaded manuscript’s distinction between gender diversity, technical participation, and technical influence, this article develops a theory-oriented framework of women’s technical agency in AI-enabled ISF. The central argument is that participation becomes consequential only when women technical professionals possess sufficient decision authority, technical autonomy, organizational voice, and access to governance processes to translate situated knowledge into technical choices. The framework integrates insights from sociotechnical systems scholarship, feminist standpoint and feminist HCI, gendered innovation, and responsible AI documentation. It proposes a staged mechanism linking technical participation to technical agency, design deliberation, and potentially more context-sensitive AI-enabled ISF. Four boundary conditions—organizational authority, technical autonomy, interdisciplinary collaboration, and governance access—are theorized as shaping whether participation becomes influence. The article contributes a construct distinction, a process model, testable qualitative propositions, and a future empirical research architecture. Because no field data have yet been collected, all propositions remain theoretically sensitizing, and no claims are made about observed organizational practice or AI outcomes.
why: Theory of women's technical agency, no implementation

title: Optimal ratcheting dividend policies with resets
abstract: We study an optimal dividend policy problem under ratcheting and bankruptcy constraints. Firms face a tradeoff between the negative signal of a dividend reduction and a potential future bankruptcy. In contrast to previous works, the dividend rate is allowed to decrease after incurring a negative impact on equity valuation in accordance with a large empirical literature on the topic. We provide an explicit necessary and sufficient condition for the finiteness of the value function and prove the differentiability of the value function, and its characterization via viscosity solutions and the so-called supercontact property. The value function is given by the solution of a two-dimensional variational inequality combining optimal stopping, singular and impulse controls. We show that the problem is equivalent to a one-dimensional setup simplifying both mathematical and financial analysis. Finally, we provide a numerical study of the model and a sensitivity analysis with respect to the model parameters. We show the relevance of over-reaction to financial news on the manager's optimal policy.
why: Pure optimal-control dividend theory, no data

title: Martingality in EFM Signature Volatility Models
abstract: We establish a martingality criterion for the Exponentially Fading Memory (EFM) signature volatility model, extending the recent result of Abi Jaber, Gassiat, and Sotnikov (2026). In the proposed framework, the volatility process is given by a linear functional of the EFM signature of a time-augmented Brownian motion, which yields a globally well-behaved, fully non-Markovian volatility model admitting a stationary distribution. The stationary EFM signature volatility model is also covered by allowing for a random initial value of the signature. Moreover, the volatility process can be adjusted to the initial forward variance curve. For this model, excluding trivial cases, we prove that the price process is a true martingale if and only if the truncation order is odd and a sign condition involving the correlation parameter holds.
why: Pure signature volatility martingale theory

title: The Architecture of Sovereignty Confronting the Clash of Matrices: Geopolitics of Franco-Caribbean Conglomerates, the Dominican Deregulated Fortress, and Real Estate Investment Resilience in the Face of the Haitian Crisis
abstract: Context and Problem Statement: The contemporary globalized economy has fractured into competing normative blocs (Destin, 2026; Rodrik, 2011; Farrell and Newman, 2019). At the geopolitical crossroads of the Americas and the Caribbean, this collision pits Latin American deregulated extractive capitalism against the Macron Matrix, which reprograms French overseas territories (Martinique, Guadeloupe, French Guiana) into normative, financial, and digital routers of European sovereignty and the Brussels Effect (Bradford, 2020; Destin, 2026). In October 2026, this asymmetry culminates on Hispaniola: while Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele launched a military operation on October 21, 2026, against armed gangs in Haiti deploying armored vehicles from the Gang Suppression Force (GSF), the Dominican Republic preserves its deregulated fortress model, where the local elite (Tutumpotes) privatizes its antifragility behind opaque fiduciary shields (Taleb, 2012; Destin, 2026). Caught between European regulatory rigidity and Caribbean kinetic volatility, Franco-Caribbean conglomerates and investors face structural vulnerability as they project supply chains and savings into the Dominican Republic to escape insular market narrowness, transfer extractivism, and the Dead Capital induced by Article 815 of the French Civil Code (De Soto, 2000; Destin, 2026). Methodology: Adopting the lens of the Geopolitics of Conglomerates and The Destin Doctrine (Destin, 2026), this study mobilizes a qualitative multiple-case study design (Yin, 2018) and comparative institutional economics (North, 1990; Coase, 1960). Purposive sampling yielded 25 Franco-Caribbean observation units (AFC1 to AFC25) operating across Martinique, Guadeloupe, and the Dominican Republic: (1) a Corporate Subgroup (AFC1-AFC10) comprising 4 construction/agro-industrial conglomerates (AFC1-AFC4), 3 energy and engineering mid-caps (AFC5-AFC7), and 3 maritime and air logistics operators at Caucedo port and regional airports (AFC8-AFC10); and (2) a Real Estate Subgroup (AFC11-AFC25) comprising 8 seasonal rental investors in Las Terrenas and Punta Cana under the CONFOTUR Law 158-01 regime (AFC11-AFC18) and 7 residential/office investors in Santo Domingo (AFC19-AFC25). Data underwent two-cycle thematic coding (Saldana, 2016) and triangulation (Denzin, 2012). Empirical Results: Corporate nearshoring to the Dominican Republic reduces supply costs by 15% to 28%, but collides with fiduciary asymmetry between mandatory European CSRD auditing (Directive 2022/2464) and opaque Dominican Fideicomisos (Law 189-11), alongside due diligence liabilities from informal Haitian labor. Furthermore, while 73% of surveyed real estate investors (AFC11-AFC25) fled Article 815 Dead Capital, the October 21, 2026 Bukele/GSF military operation in Haiti exposed three vulnerabilities: (i) border militarization and deportations of Haitian construction workers triggered 12-to-18-month delivery delays; (ii) gang spillover fears drove an 18% to 25% surge in private security costs, compressing net rental yields from 8.5% to below 5.2%; and (iii) European AMLD/TRACFIN bank filters freeze USD/DOP rent repatriations. Conclusion: Executives and investors must transition toward Sovereignty Engineering via three imperatives (Destin, 2026): (1) Insular Land Securitization (TFI) through hybrid French SAS holdings governed by DACH-style Cold Governance co-investing in CSRD-audited bank Fideicomisos; (2) monetizing the role of European Normative Router; and (3) avoiding organizational Universe 25 behavioral sinks (Calhoun, 1973) by deploying clinical seismography and a cybernetic AI Exocortex for kinetic risk governance.
why: Geopolitical real-estate theory, no finance ML implementation

title: A Cloud-Native Dynamic Pricing Engine for Shared Public-Private Parking Ecosystems Using Demand Forecasting
abstract: Urban parking management systems continue to rely on static pricing schemes even though demand for parking facilities changes over time by peak hours, day of the week, changing weather conditions in the relevant area, and nearby special events. Since parking facilities have been underpriced during high-demand peak hours and overpriced during offpeak hours, this leads to underutilized parking spaces and loss of revenue for parking operators. The proposed research framework, based on historical parking transaction data collected from Seattle, USA, was combined with weather and event-signal data to develop a forecasting pipeline. Considering both tabular and sequential data, seven forecasting models were evaluated, including Histogram Gradient Boosting Regressor, XGBoost Regressor, Random Forest Regressor, LSTM, CNN-LSTM, LSTM-GRU, and Transformer. Bounded dynamic prices were generated using a ratio-based approach, and the entire pricing engine was evaluated with metrics of forecast accuracy, simulated business revenue, price stability, and compliance with operational fairness attributes. This study demonstrates its novelty compared to previous studies by combining four aspects of demand forecasting, a bound-controlled dynamic pricing engine, multi-criteria operational evaluation, and integrated cloud-native deployment into a single framework. The evaluated results demonstrated that no single forecasting model performed consistently in both the forecast accuracy and the business operational constraints. The highest-performing models were CNN-LSTM in forecasting accuracy, Random Forest for simulated revenue on a parking facility, and LSTM-GRU in pricing stability and operational fairness. The transformer was in the highest position by multilevel evaluation under all dimensions, demonstrating that the overall dynamic pricing engine for the parking ecosystem should be evaluated by considering both demand forecasting accuracy and operational performance. The selected cloud service deployment was evaluated using 300 API requests, resulting in a 100% success rate with a 5.11 s mean latency and a 4.53 s median latency.
why: Seattle parking demand forecasting, not financial

title: Financing Innovation: Modernizing the Qualified Small Business Stock Rules
abstract: Congress’s recent expansion of the Qualified Small Business Stock (“QSBS”) tax exclusion through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act has shifted the debate surrounding this longstanding incentive. Rather than scaling back what some scholars consider an outdated incentive, Congress reaffirmed QSBS as a central component of the government’s plan to encourage entrepreneurial investment. But in doing so, Congress failed to adequately consider how this provision should evolve to more effectively advance Congress’s objective of encouraging long-term investment in innovative businesses. This Article argues that the rules governing QSBS contained in Section 1202 of the Internal Revenue Code have become increasingly misaligned with the modern innovation economy. Enacted in 1993, the provision was designed around an economic model in which high-growth businesses accumulated value through tangible assets, scaled through conventional business models, and operated as traditional C corporations. However, today many innovative companies increasingly derive substantial value from software, artificial intelligence, data, intellectual property, and other intangible assets. Yet Section 1202 continues to condition one of the Code’s most valuable tax incentives on eligibility rules that no longer reflect how high-growth businesses are formed, financed, or create value. As a result, the statute distorts organizational decisions, misallocates tax incentives, and excludes many of the businesses Congress intended to encourage. This Article develops a framework for modernizing Section 1202 while remaining faithful to Congress’ original purpose of incentivizing high-growth investments. It proposes three principal reforms: updating the qualified trade or business limitation to reflect contemporary models of value creation, replacing the gross asset test with a three-year aggregate gross receipts test, and expanding eligibility beyond C corporations to accommodate modern startup formation and financing practices. Together, these reforms would better align Section 1202 with the realities of today’s entrepreneurial economy while preserving its core objective of encouraging long-term investment in innovative, high-growth businesses.
why: US tax statute analysis, no ML or data

title: MbEBC (EnergiaBeneComune): Investment, Return (IRR) and Value (MbVEL) of a Distributed Solar-Hydrogen System in 26 European Union Countries
abstract: This paper applies MbVEL (Value = Energy + Labour) to the MbEBC (EnergiaBeneComune) model: a distributed system of photovoltaics (PV), blade-less wind, electrolysers, hydrogen (H2) tanks and already existing turbines that brings the cost of energy towards 0 and, at equal value, leaves room for higher pay. MbVEL is the main work; MbEBC tests its physical and financial feasibility and also answers how to do it. The elements of MbEBC are MbVEL-2, MbVEL-3, MbVEL-4 and MbVEL-5. Revenues are the market value of the energy produced by PV (MbVEL-2 and MbVEL-3, which add up), of offshore wind (MbVEL-5) and, with heat, of hydrogen (MbVEL-4). With 500 €/kW for PV and inverter, 250 €/kW for the electrolyser, tanks simulated with biomethane tanks and sized on the daily cycle, prices without taxes and average household and business network costs, the IRR (average annual return on capital, net of 30-year amortisation) exceeds the WACC (Weighted Average Cost of Capital) in 20 of 26 countries with available prices: for example Italy 21.3% against 6.46%, France 13.2% against 5.18%, Germany 10.2% against 3.79%. Without public contributions the premise does not hold in 6 countries (Estonia, Finland, Poland, Romania, Sweden, Hungary). With the 2023 public environmental transfers (25 countries with data, Eurostat) the investment on the national potential would be covered in 4.3 years in Italy (a figure dominated by a one-off energy-saving transfer), 9.6 in Germany and 50.4 in France, and in more than 100 years in 8 countries. How much should be installed each year of panels, electrolysers, tanks and turbines in two phases is also computed: short (MbVEL-2 and the hydrogen chain) and long (MbVEL-3). With offshore wind (MbVEL-5) and hydrogen the model shows that fossil fuels (gas, oil, coal) for electricity and road transport can be replaced, with declared rules and costs; the weighted average cost is 75.2-82.6 €/MWh during amortisation and 16.8 after; Section 9 also shows where the thesis does not hold without grants and leaves to each State, through a European referendum, the political choice of who manages the value created. AI-use statement: The original idea of the Value = Energy + Labour indicator and of the EnergiaBeneComune model is the author's, Marco Bava, as are the considerations collected in the preparatory document "Trilogia economica dell'idrogeno". Data collection, calculations and drafting were carried out with the assistance of an artificial intelligence assistant (Claude, Anthropic); the author reviewed the contents and is solely responsible for the work.
why: Solar-hydrogen IRR model, not AI finance

title: Differentiability and Convexity of the Solution Maps for Fully Non-linear Parabolic HJB Equations
abstract: We study the dependence on the terminal condition of solutions to a fully nonlinear parabolic Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman (HJB) equation, when the terminal condition varies along a finite-dimensional family. This problem is motivated by a dual formulation of semimartingale optimal transport. The equation is posed as a terminal-value Cauchy problem on an unbounded spatial domain. Under structural ellipticity and regularity assumptions on the nonlinear operator, we recall local parabolic Hölder estimates and stability results for bounded uniformly continuous terminal data. We then establish continuous directional differentiability of the solution map with respect to the finite-dimensional parameter, and identify its derivative through the corresponding linearized Cauchy problem. Under an additional convexity assumption on the Hamiltonian and a non-degeneracy condition on the terminal data, we prove local strong convexity of the point-evaluated solution map. The analysis relies on Evans--Krylov theory for fully nonlinear parabolic equations and combines PDE arguments with probabilistic representations. Finally, we extend the differentiability and convexity results to cascades of Cauchy problems in which successive equations are coupled through terminal conditions at several prescribed times. This structure is motivated, for instance, by optimal transport problems with marginal constraints imposed at several maturities.
why: Pure HJB equation theory, no data or implementation
